title: How moving water changes the land

files.lesson.md: --- order: 4 unit: water title: How moving water changes the land node: AC9HG7K01 n4 summary: Explain erosion, transport and deposition as processes that change a place, rather than merely naming a landform. language: maths hook: A river runs through a valley. Does that explain how the valley became deeper? --- Water flowing downhill gains energy as gravity pulls it down a slope. It can loosen and remove soil or rock: **erosion**. It can carry material along: **transport**. When flow slows enough that it cannot carry some material, particles settle: **deposition**. The carried particles are **sediment**. A process explanation says how a place changes. Naming a valley or saying a river is there does not explain how water changes the land. ## Predict: after the storm ```step stage: predict insight: Predict removal and accumulation from the same flow. check: type: predict q: In made-up Kerrin, storm runoff crosses a bare slope and enters the lake. What might you find afterwards? options: - A small channel on the slope and soil deposited near the lake entrance - Only water has moved, so the land cannot have changed - All the loosened soil remains exactly where it started - A taller slope because water added material everywhere actual: Runoff can remove soil, carry it to the lake and let some settle as flow slows. ``` ## Try: name what happened ```step stage: run insight: Distinguish erosion, transport and deposition. check: type: match q: Match the made-up observations to the process. pairs: - - Runoff cuts soil out of a bare slope - Erosion - - Flow carries loosened soil towards the lake - Transport - - Particles settle where flow enters the lake and slows - Deposition explain: Material can be removed in one place and added elsewhere. ``` ## Worked example: a process, not a location ```step stage: investigate insight: Explain change through water acting on material. tasks: - check: type: question q: Which order explains Kerrin’s storm? options: - Downhill flow → erosion → transport → deposition - Downhill flow → deposition → erosion → transport - Downhill flow → transport → deposition → erosion - Deposition → downhill flow → erosion → transport answer: 0 feedback: - null - Soil must be removed and carried before it settles elsewhere. - Removal comes before carrying that material towards the lake. - Start with moving water; settling is the final part of this case. explain: Gravity pulls runoff downhill. Flow removes soil, carries it and deposits some where it slows. - check: type: bug code: working.txt#nib text: Nib explains the case. Click the first line where the reasoning goes wrong. answer: 3 fault: logic misconception: valley-location-is-process explain: Line 3 gives the river’s location as the whole explanation. Explain how erosion and transport remove material over time. smaller: check: type: question q: A marked patch of soil is gone after runoff carries it away. Which process removed it? options: - Erosion - Deposition answer: 0 feedback: - null - Deposition adds material; this patch lost it. explain: Erosion removes material from a place. hint: - Does Nib explain a change or name a location? - Look for what happens to soil or rock. - A process explanation says how material is removed. ``` ### Build the process chain ### Find Nib’s slip ```worked \text{Energy} :: Gravity pulls runoff down a bare slope in a made-up park. \text{Erosion} :: Water removes loose soil. \text{Transport} :: Flow carries the soil along a shallow channel. \text{Change} :: The slope loses soil and the channel becomes deeper. ``` ## Vary: changed flow, changed channel ```step stage: modify insight: Apply the process to a sourced river and a made-up deposit. tasks: - check: type: question q: On the Snowy River card, what process changes the channel? options: - Released flows scour and carry sediment from the bed - The river’s location alone explains its changing depth - All the sediment stays fixed once it reaches the river - The river’s name tells us how its channel was formed answer: 0 feedback: - null - Location omits the process acting on the material. - Flow can pick up and carry sediment from the bed. - A name does not explain physical change. explain: Scouring removes material and flow transports it, reshaping the channel. - check: type: question q: Why might a deposit form where runoff enters Kerrin’s lake? options: - Flow slows enough for some carried particles to settle - The water must vanish as soon as it enters the lake - All carried soil instantly turns into dissolved salt - Deposition lifts material off the slope upstream answer: 0 feedback: - null - Water can keep moving while particles settle. - Sediment need not dissolve to move or settle. - That describes removal, not settling. explain: Deposition occurs when flow can no longer carry some of its sediment. ``` ### A real riverbed NSW Environment and Heritage describes **Snowy River** environmental releases scouring (washing away) and transporting sediment to help form a deeper channel within the old riverbed. This is a real example of water changing a place by removing and moving sediment. *Source: [Managing water for the environment: Snowy and montane rivers (NSW Environment and Heritage)](https://www.environment.nsw.gov.au/topics/water/water-for-the-environment/catchments/snowy-and-montane/managing), checked 30 October 2026.* ### A made-up deposit ## Practise: explain the change ```step stage: practise insight: Use process terms instead of merely naming outcomes. tasks: - check: type: sort q: In these made-up observations, which process is the main focus? options: - Erosion - Transport - Deposition items: - - A stream removes soil from its bank - Erosion - Material is removed from the bank. - - Sand travels along the streambed - Transport - The focus is material being carried. - - Silt settles on a flooded field as water slows - Deposition - Settling adds material at this place. - check: type: question q: Which explanation tells how a valley can become deeper? options: - Repeated flows erode the bed and carry loosened material away - The river lies in a low place between areas of higher ground - The valley is below a hill and the river is at its bottom - A valley is a low area with a river flowing through it answer: 0 feedback: - null - This locates the river but does not explain the change. - Relative height is an observation, not a process. - A definition does not explain removal of material. explain: Erosion and transport can deepen a channel over time. ``` ### Which process? ### Explain, rather than locate ## Make: how a place changed ```step stage: make insight: Explain one physical change with appropriate process terms. check: type: reflect text: In my own book I explained how runoff changed Kerrin’s bare slope using erosion and transport. I identified the removed material and where water carries it. A partner or teacher read it. ``` Use the storm from Predict. Draw a before-and-after sketch and write a short explanation naming the slope, flowing water, soil removed and material carried away. Write in your book, not on this page. ## Typical: where material builds up ```step stage: make insight: Explain deposition as well as removal in the same case. check: type: reflect text: I added the lake entrance to my Kerrin explanation and explained why some sediment settles there, using erosion, transport and deposition accurately. tier: typical ``` Material lost from the slope can be gained at the lake entrance. A river can both erode and deposit; do not give it one permanent label. ## Wider: change the ground cover ```step stage: make insight: Apply the chain to another surface at the same level. check: type: reflect text: I compared two made-up slopes with the same rain and steepness, one with plant cover and one with exposed loose soil. I explained which could lose more soil and why. tier: wider ``` Imagine roots and ground cover protect the first slope. Loose soil on the second is exposed to runoff. Explain a possible difference and another condition you would need to check. Typical and wider steps are extras on the same idea. You do not need them to finish the lesson. ```teacher summary: Explain erosion, transport and deposition as processes that change a place, rather than merely naming a landform. time: 40 timing: Predict and Try 8 min · Worked example 12 min · Vary 8 min · Practise 6 min · Make 6 min. Optional width is extra. goals: - I can explain how flowing water removes and carries material. - I can distinguish erosion, transport and deposition. - I can explain a physical change instead of just naming a landform. struggle: Students may say the river found a valley as if location were a process. Ask what is removed, what carries it and how the place looks different. before: "Usually Year 7. Minimum Make explains one change process: runoff eroding a slope and carrying soil away. A complete removal-to-deposition explanation is optional width. Kerrin, storms, valleys and cover comparisons are made up. The sourced Snowy River channel replaces an unchecked story about formation of a particular mountain valley. River valleys may have complex histories; do not imply one storm makes a large valley or all valleys are formed by rivers. Flow speed is not the only condition affecting sediment movement: particle size, discharge and sediment supply matter." running: - "Try: ask whether the place gains or loses material." - "Worked example: order the chain before discussing Nib." - "Vary: connect scour with removal and transport with carrying." - "Make: expect water acting on named material, not only a labelled sketch." stuck: - see: A valley is named with no process. ask: What happens to soil or rock, and where does it go? fix: Add erosion and transport to explain change. - see: Erosion and deposition are swapped. ask: Does the place lose or gain material? fix: Removal is erosion; settling adds material by deposition. - see: All flowing water is said to deposit. ask: Can this flow keep carrying these particles? fix: Settling depends on whether flow can carry the material. support: Use the smaller removal question. Act out remove, carry, settle with three cards, then return to the picture. stretch: Change ground cover in the invented case, keeping the same process explanation. exit: q: Why is the river is in a low place not enough to explain a deepening valley? a: It gives location, not a process. Flow erodes soil or rock and transports it away; repeated removal can deepen the channel. explain: Erosion removes material, transport carries it, and deposition adds sediment where it settles. Explain water acting on material and the resulting change to a place. sources: - title: "Managing water for the environment: Snowy and montane rivers (NSW Environment and Heritage)" url: https://www.environment.nsw.gov.au/topics/water/water-for-the-environment/catchments/snowy-and-montane/managing checked: 2026-10-30 leads: "Next: classification, connection and change together. Optional width stays on the same process, with no older-year geomorphology." class: inquiry: q: If a river takes soil away from one place, has the material vanished? prompts: - What is your reason? - What information would change your view? notes: Follow material through removal, carrying and settling. A location alone cannot explain physical change. activities: - at: investigate kind: discussion title: Remove, carry, settle minutes: 5 do: Pairs trace soil through Kerrin’s storm. Where is it removed, carried and deposited? The listener identifies the missing process in Nib’s explanation. notes: Follow material through removal, carrying and settling. A location alone cannot explain physical change. - at: make kind: activity title: Compare your explanations minutes: 4 do: Write in your own book, then swap with a partner. The partner identifies the geographical terms and one link explained with because. notes: The reflect tick records completion. The teacher or partner reads the writing; the site does not assess it. ```
